tldr: Cimadamore and Klang explain method handles as 'link once, execute many' and trace that idea through reflection, string concatenation, FFM downcalls and a planned marshalling API.
summary: Cimadamore starts from core reflection. Calling Point.translate via Method.invoke boxes arguments into an Object array, checks access through @CallerSensitive, unboxes and only then calls, on every invocation; his benchmark put it at about a third of a direct call's throughput. The JVM splits a call into linkage (resolution, access check, vtable index) and execution, and method handles, added in Java 7 with invokedynamic, expose that split. A Lookup checks access once at creation; invokeExact is signature-polymorphic, so javac burns the static argument and cast types into the call site, leaving a cheap type check. Since Java 18, java.lang.reflect.Method wraps a method handle, closing most of the gap.

The same pattern repeats. Pre-Java 9 string concatenation compiled to StringBuilder chains whose default capacity of 16 always resized for his 21-character example. Since Java 9, javac emits an invokedynamic call to StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants with a recipe; the generated code precomputes the constant length and coder, then sizes one byte array exactly, which he said made concatenation about twice as fast. In the Foreign Function & Memory API, a downcall handle points not at bytecode but at an assembly trampoline generated once from a FunctionDescriptor of memory layouts, following the platform ABI. jextract can generate the wrappers so users never touch the handles.

Klang then shows his exploratory work on marshalling as a successor to serialization: a class declares explicit structural versions as records (PointV1) that map to and from the real type. A naive reflective marshaller redoes type inspection and access checks for every object; instead, a schema with marshal and unmarshal method handles is generated once per type and cached, and his rough benchmark favoured handles by a wide margin. With Project Leyden, that linkage could move to a training run. In Q&A they named string templates as the next likely user, said combinator-heavy handles generate bloat so the JDK often spins classes with the class-file API, and mentioned Project Babylon.
keyPoints: Method.invoke boxes arguments, checks access via @CallerSensitive and unboxes on every call; a method handle does the access check once through MethodHandles.Lookup.
invokeExact is signature-polymorphic: javac encodes the static argument types and the cast return type into the call site descriptor, so no boxing or varargs array is needed.
A static final method handle is a JIT constant, so the remaining type check is effectively a pointer comparison.
Since Java 18, core reflection is reimplemented on top of method handles, so reflective calls reuse the same C2 optimisations.
Indy string concatenation (Java 9) uses makeConcatWithConstants with a recipe string, precomputing constant length and encoding (coder), then filling one exactly sized byte array.
FFM downcall handles are built from a symbol address and a FunctionDescriptor; the ABI classification and assembly trampoline are generated once at creation.
Klang's marshalling prototype caches a per-type schema with marshal and unmarshal method handles; with Project Leyden this linking could happen at training time.
Combinator-heavy method handle trees generate a lot of hidden bytecode; JDK code such as string concatenation moved to spinning one class with the class-file API instead.
takeaways: Store method handles in static final fields and call them with invokeExact using exact static types and a cast on the result.
In your own framework code, separate one-time setup (lookup, type analysis, access checks) from the per-call path and cache the result.
Use jextract to generate FFM bindings instead of writing downcall handles by hand.
Prefer generating a single class with the class-file API over deep method handle combinator chains when the shape is complex.

watchIf: You write frameworks, serializers or native interop code and want to understand why the JDK keeps reaching for method handles and how to get their performance.
